lesson.title: One to Many, On Purpose: How Multicast Avoids Wasteful Copies
lesson.summary: Multicast lets one sender deliver a single stream of packets to a group of interested receivers, addressed to a shared group IP address, so the network replicates traffic only at the points where it actually needs to branch.
lesson.body:
Unicast solves one-to-one delivery well but breaks down when many receivers want the identical content at the same time, because sending separate unicast copies to each one wastes bandwidth in proportion to the number of receivers. Multicast solves this by introducing a different kind of address: instead of identifying a single host, a multicast address identifies a group that any interested host can choose to join. The sender transmits one stream addressed to that group address, and it is the network's job, not the sender's, to deliver copies only to the routers and links that actually lead toward a group member, replicating the packet at branch points rather than at the source.

In IPv4, multicast addresses form their own reserved range, 224.0.0.0 through 239.255.255.255, distinct from the unicast addresses used for individual hosts. Hosts announce their interest in receiving a particular group's traffic using the Internet Group Management Protocol, IGMP, which lets a host tell its local router that it wants packets sent to a particular group address. Routers then use a separate protocol, commonly Protocol Independent Multicast, PIM, to build and maintain the distribution trees across the network that carry multicast traffic only along paths that actually lead to at least one interested receiver.

Routing protocols themselves lean on multicast for exactly the efficiency it provides. OSPF routers send their Hello packets to the multicast address 224.0.0.5, a reserved group meaning all OSPF routers on that link. Every OSPF-speaking router on the segment is already listening for that group address, so a single Hello reaches all of them without the sending router needing to know or address each neighbor individually, and without flooding the packet to every host on the segment regardless of whether it cares about OSPF at all.

The underlying network layer machinery here is the same forwarding logic covered under unicast, matching a destination address against forwarding state and sending the packet onward, but the addressing model and the fact that the network itself performs replication rather than the sender is what makes multicast fundamentally different. Multicast trades some added complexity in routers, since they must track group membership and build distribution trees, for a large efficiency win whenever the same content genuinely needs to reach many destinations, IPTV distribution and video conferencing among the common uses.

Multicast also has a narrower reach than unicast in practice. A block of that reserved address range, 224.0.0.0 through 224.0.0.255, is set aside specifically for link-local control traffic, meaning packets sent to those addresses, like the OSPF Hello example, are never forwarded beyond the local network segment by design, regardless of how routers are otherwise configured. More broadly, true multicast routing across the public internet, spanning many independently operated networks, was never widely adopted, largely because it requires every network along the path to cooperate in tracking group membership and building shared distribution trees, with no obvious way for each network to bill for the traffic it carries on another provider's behalf. As a result, multicast today is mostly deployed within single administrative domains, an enterprise network, a cable provider's IPTV infrastructure, or a data center, rather than end to end across the open internet the way unicast routinely is.
